prompt: `az group create` with no parameters answers `the following arguments are required`. Who refused?
hint: Did anything leave the computer?

choices.text: Resource Manager, which needs a name for every group
choices.why: No request was sent; Resource Manager never saw it.

choices.text: The CLI itself, while reading the line
choices.why: Right. Parsing happens before any sign-in or request.

choices.text: Microsoft Entra ID, for want of a sign-in
choices.why: A missing sign-in gives `Please run 'az login'`, a different stop.

choices.text: Azure Policy, which requires names to follow a convention
choices.why: Policy is judged in Resource Manager, which this command never reached.

prompt: The help for `--location` ends with `Config: brazilsouth.`. What does that tell you?
hint: Which setting does `env.sh` export?

choices.text: That `brazilsouth` is the only region the lab supports
choices.why: Any region can be named on the line; this is only the fallback.

choices.text: That the subscription was created in São Paulo
choices.why: A subscription has no location, and the lab has none at all.

choices.text: That a default location is set and will fill the parameter
choices.why: Right. It came from `AZURE_DEFAULTS_LOCATION`.

choices.text: That `--location` is required for this command
choices.why: Only `--name` was marked `[Required]`.

prompt: `az config get defaults` lists `group` with the source `/home/ana/azure/.azure/config`. Where did that value come from?
hint: Which command writes that file?

choices.text: From an `az config set` someone ran
choices.why: Right. It writes the configuration file inside `AZURE_CONFIG_DIR`.

choices.text: From `env.sh`, like the location
choices.why: `env.sh` exports only the location; its source reads `AZURE_DEFAULTS_LOCATION`.

choices.text: From the last resource group the CLI created
choices.why: The CLI does not remember what it created as a default.

choices.text: From the subscription's own settings in Azure
choices.why: A path on disk is a local file, not something read from Azure.

prompt: A deploy script runs `az group delete --yes` and relies on the default group. Last week a colleague ran `az config set defaults.group=rg-shop-prod` in the same CLI. What is the lesson's advice?
hint: Which of the three places wins?

choices.text: Export `AZURE_DEFAULTS_GROUP` in the script, which outranks the file
choices.why: It would win, but it is still a default the next person may change; naming the group is safer.

choices.text: Run `az config unset` at the start of every script
choices.why: It removes one default and leaves the script still depending on whatever else is set.

choices.text: Nothing: `--yes` asks for confirmation before deleting
choices.why: `--yes` does the opposite: it skips the confirmation.

choices.text: Name the group on the command line every time
choices.why: Right. A parameter on the line always wins, and does not depend on anybody's defaults.

prompt: Order the three places a setting can come from, from the one that loses to the one that wins.
hint: The one closest to the command wins.
items: a parameter on the command line
trap: The environment variable beats the file, which is why `env.sh` could set the location without touching it.

prompt: Where does an extension installed with `az extension add` land in this lab?
hint: What did `env.sh` set aside for the CLI?

choices.text: In `~/azure/venv`, beside the CLI's own packages
choices.why: Extensions are kept apart from the installation, so an upgrade does not lose them.

choices.text: Nowhere: extensions run in Azure, not locally
choices.why: An extension is a Python package the CLI loads on your computer.

choices.text: In `/usr/lib`, shared by every user
choices.why: Nothing in this lab is installed system-wide except Ubuntu's packages.

choices.text: Inside `AZURE_CONFIG_DIR`, in `~/azure/.azure`
choices.why: Right. So the lab's extensions are separate from any other CLI on the machine.

prompt: To see every step the CLI takes, including each request and response, add `--___` to the command.
hint: The same word as a programmer's tool for finding bugs.

prompt: Which `--output` format is meant for shell scripts?
hint: No keys, no quotes.

choices.text: `table`
choices.why: Its column widths depend on the data, which breaks parsing.

choices.text: `jsonc`
choices.why: Its colour codes break a pipe.

choices.text: `tsv`
choices.why: Right. Values separated by tabs, with nothing around them.

choices.text: `yaml`
choices.why: Readable, but a script would have to parse YAML.

prompt: Why did `--query "[?name=='AzureCloud'].endpoints.resourceManager | [0]" --output tsv` print a bare address with no brackets?
hint: What does `| [0]` do to a list?

choices.text: Because `| [0]` turned the one-entry list into its value
choices.why: Right. The filter returned a list, and `[0]` took its first entry.

choices.text: Because `tsv` removes brackets from any list
choices.why: `tsv` prints a list as several lines, not as a single value.

choices.text: Because only one cloud is active
choices.why: The filter was on the name, not on `isActive`.

choices.text: Because `endpoints` is never a list in JMESPath
choices.why: It is an object; the list came from the filter in front of it.

prompt: Match each JMESPath piece to what it does.
hint: One of them builds something new.

pairs.right: keep the entries where the test is true
build a new object from chosen fields
refer to a field rather than its value

prompt: A query written as `--query '[?name=="AzureCloud"].name'` fails with an error about a field. What is the lesson's rule?
hint: In JMESPath, which quotes make a string?

choices.text: JMESPath does not support filters on names
choices.why: It does: the lesson's own filter compares `name`.

choices.text: Double quotes outside, single quotes for strings inside
choices.why: Right. In JMESPath double quotes name a field, so `"AzureCloud"` was read as one.

choices.text: The query must end in `| [0]`
choices.why: `| [0]` is for taking one value, not for making a filter work.

choices.text: Queries only work with `--output tsv`
choices.why: `--query` works with every output format.

prompt: A script runs `az account list --query "[0].id" -o tsv` and stores the result as the subscription to deploy to. In a terminal nobody signed in to, what happens?
hint: What did `az account list` answer in the lab, and with which exit code?

choices.text: The command fails, and a script with `set -e` stops at once
choices.why: It did not fail: it exited with 0.

choices.text: The CLI opens a browser to sign in first
choices.why: Only `az login` does that; this command just warns.

choices.text: It gets an empty value and carries on, with exit code 0
choices.why: Right. An empty list is a correct answer, so the script must check what came back.

choices.text: It picks the subscription named in `env.sh`
choices.why: `env.sh` names no subscription.

prompt: You have a compiled `main.json` and want its resource types. Which tool does the lesson say to use?
hint: Is a file the answer of an `az` command?

choices.text: `az --query`, which accepts a file name
choices.why: `--query` works only on the answer of the command it is given to.

choices.text: `jq`, since the template is a file and not a CLI answer
choices.why: Right. `--query` for an `az` answer, `jq` for everything else.

choices.text: `grep` on the `table` output
choices.why: There is no `table` of a file, and parsing a table is the thing to avoid.

choices.text: `az bicep build --query`
choices.why: Building prints a template; it is not a JSON answer the CLI filters.

prompt: The query language behind `--query` is called ___.
hint: Its name starts with JMES.

prompt: What is the Azure PowerShell equivalent of `az group list`?
hint: Verb-noun, with `Az` in the noun.

choices.text: `List-AzGroup`
choices.why: `List` is not one of PowerShell's verbs; `Get` is.

choices.text: `az-group-list`
choices.why: That is the CLI's command with dashes, not a cmdlet.

choices.text: `Show-AzureGroups`
choices.why: The module's nouns start with `Az` and are singular.

choices.text: `Get-AzResourceGroup`
choices.why: Right. `Get` reads, and the noun names the type.

prompt: What is the difference between the Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell that the lesson says matters?
hint: Look at what comes back.

choices.text: PowerShell returns objects, the CLI prints text
choices.why: Right. Choose by what your team already writes.

choices.text: PowerShell reaches services the CLI cannot
choices.why: Both reach the same API, so neither can do what the other cannot.

choices.text: The CLI is faster because it skips Resource Manager
choices.why: Neither skips it; both send their requests through Resource Manager.

choices.text: PowerShell runs only on Windows
choices.why: PowerShell 7 runs on Linux and macOS too.

prompt: Which of these are true of Cloud Shell, by Microsoft's documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the machine, the storage and the account.

choices.text: A session ends after 20 minutes without interactive activity
choices.why: Right. The machine is temporary.

choices.text: It keeps `$HOME` on a 5 GB file share in your own storage account
choices.why: Right, and that storage is billed at normal rates.

choices.text: It works without an Azure account
choices.why: It opens from the portal, signed in as you.

choices.text: It is already signed in with the identity you used for the portal
choices.why: Right. That is what makes it handy for five minutes.

choices.text: Software installed outside `$HOME` survives to the next session
choices.why: The machine is replaced; only `$HOME` persists, and only with storage.

prompt: Ana keeps production and staging apart by signing in to each in a separate terminal, each with its own `AZURE_CONFIG_DIR`. What does that arrangement protect against?
hint: What does a CLI that never signed in to staging know about it?

choices.text: Against a token being stolen from the disk
choices.why: Each directory still holds a token; the arrangement is about mistakes, not theft.

choices.text: Against pointing a command at the wrong subscription by mistake
choices.why: Right. The production terminal cannot reach staging at all.

choices.text: Against throttling, since each directory has its own limit
choices.why: Limits are counted per subscription and region in Azure, not per directory.

choices.text: Against needing multifactor authentication twice
choices.why: Two sign-ins mean two second factors, not fewer.

prompt: `az network vnet create` is typed without `--location`, in a terminal that read `env.sh`. Where would the network go?
hint: Which default does `env.sh` export?

choices.text: To `southcentralus`, São Paulo's pair
choices.why: The pair has nothing to do with defaults.

choices.text: Nowhere: the command is refused without a location
choices.why: A default fills it, as the help said with `Config:`.

choices.text: To the region of the subscription
choices.why: A subscription has no region of its own.

choices.text: To `brazilsouth`
choices.why: Right. `AZURE_DEFAULTS_LOCATION` fills the missing parameter.

prompt: A script parses `az vm list --output table` with `awk '{print $2}'` and works for months, then breaks. What is the likeliest cause the lesson warns about?
hint: What decides a table's layout?

choices.text: A new value changed the columns
choices.why: Right. Widths and columns follow the data, so ask for fields with `--query` and use `tsv`.

choices.text: Microsoft removed `--output table`
choices.why: It still exists; the layout is what changed.

choices.text: `awk` cannot read output from Python programs
choices.why: `awk` reads any text; the problem is which text arrives.

choices.text: The VM list became too long for a pipe
choices.why: A pipe has no length limit that matters here.

prompt: Put what happens to an `az` command's answer in order.
hint: The format comes last.
items: the CLI receives the JSON answer
`--output` prints that part in the chosen format
trap: Both steps after the first run on your computer, after the answer arrived.

prompt: To make a command print nothing when only its exit code matters, use `--output ___`.
hint: The word for nothing.
